newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel demands Egypt remove "threatening cloud".
newsitem.headline: Israel demands Egypt remove "threatening cloud".

text.p: Israel's new right-wing government, caught in a diplomatic row with Arab states, demanded on Tuesday that Egypt stop "threatening" it for taking a slower approach to peace than the ousted Labour administration.

Asked if Egypt could play a key peacemaking role in the present atmosphere, Foreign Minister David Levy told reporters: "If Egypt continues to express itself this way, it is effectively not interested."
Afterwards Levy said Israel expected Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to change the atmosphere. He demanded Egypt "break up this threatening cloud."

Levy summoned Egyptian Ambassador Mohammed Bassiouny to his office to complain about heightened rhetoric levelled against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Likud-led government which took office three months ago.

They met just as the London-based Arabic newspaper Asharq al-Awsat quoted Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, in the latest salvo, as saying Israel's expectations from peace talks were "nonsense," plausible only to the ignorant or mad.

Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh rushed to Netanyahu's defence, insisting the government was conducting negotiations with Palestinians "more carefully", "more responsibly" and "not as quickly" as the left-centre government it ousted.

As progress, Naveh cited a series of meetings between Israeli and Palestinian leaders. But Bassiouny said he hoped a joint Israeli-Palestinian steering committee meeting on Thursday would lead to "tangible steps on the ground."

Egypt, which in 1979 became the first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel, has complained about Israel's failure to hand over parts of the West Bank city of Hebron to self-rule as agreed in peace deals or to expand talks with Palestinians.
President Mubarak had welcomed Netanyahu when they first met in Cairo shortly after the Israeli leader took office. The Egyptian president said at the time he had "great hopes."
But Egypt's mood soured with a lack of progress in peace talks, and it threatened to cancel a Middle East economic conference scheduled for Cairo in November.

Last week Netanyahu said that to cancel the conference would hurt Cairo. Educated in the United States, he used an English expression, likening any Egyptian cancellation to "a man who cuts off his nose to spite his face."
At the time Moussa reacted angrily, calling Netanyahu's comment "unfortunate" and warning Netanyahu: "He'd do best to keep off Egypt's nose so that Egypt keeps off his nose."
"It could be the standards with the Arab world require use of terms which are less problematic from the standpoint of the Arab world," Likud Tourism Minister Moshe Katzav acknowledged on Tuesday.
On Monday, Moussa's assistant foreign minister, Fathi el-Shazli said Israeli leaders were talking like "dinosaurs" about the situation in the Middle East and were amateur politicians.
Bassiouny denied it was Egyptian policy to attack personalities. He said Egypt would express its views freely because having a peace treaty didn't mean the two countries had to agree on everything.
He said an atmosphere of peace was necessary for the economic conference -- aimed at integrating Israel into the regional economy -- to succeed.
"How can you convince the foreign investors to invest in this area in which there is no stability?" he aksed.
